group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 48-year-old man arrived in the emergency department by private vehicle late in the evening of the seventh day of an influenza-like illness that had recently evolved into high-grade fevers and a productive cough. He ordinarily works as a warehouse supervisor and is active enough to unload small pallets himself, but over the past two days he found that walking even half the length of an aisle left him markedly short of breath and forced him to pause to catch his breath while leaning on the pallet jack. Earlier that afternoon a coworker measured an oral temperature of 40 °C with a warehouse first-aid kit thermometer; acetaminophen 500 mg was suggested but never taken because the patient felt too nauseated to swallow pills. He has a background of systolic ventricular dysfunction discovered three years ago after a viral myocarditis; the most recent outpatient echocardiogram, performed six weeks before this presentation, documented an ejection fraction of 32 % with a small, stable left ventricular thrombus for which he remains on apixaban. His cardiologist last adjusted his carvedilol to 25 mg twice daily and initiated low-dose torsemide for occasional pedal edema; no changes had been made in the preceding month, and he had not missed any heart-failure medications according to a pill count performed by his spouse yesterday. Past medical history is also notable for a right testicular seminoma resected twelve years ago followed by adjuvant radiotherapy; surveillance imaging has shown no recurrence, and he has required no oncologic treatment since. He denies prior transient ischemic attacks or strokes, has never been told he has cirrhosis or hepatitis, and his creatinine has consistently been within normal limits on routine laboratory panels. He quit smoking cigarettes fifteen years ago after a 10-pack-year exposure and drinks two beers on weekends; there is no illicit drug use. Immunizations are up to date except he declined this season’s influenza vaccine because of scheduling conflicts. Approximately four days ago his cough, initially dry, began producing yellow sputum streaked with rust, and he developed chills severe enough that his wife could see the bed shaking. She noted that he breathed rapidly even while speaking in short phrases and that his lips looked a shade paler than usual. Concerned about progressive respiratory distress, she drove him to the hospital without activating emergency medical services so that no prehospital oxygen or intravenous fluids would confound baseline measurements. In triage he sat upright on the gurney, answered questions in full sentences, and was oriented to person, place, time, and current events. Prior to any antipyretics, bronchodilators, supplemental oxygen, or intravenous therapy, his vital signs were recorded as follows: oral temperature 39.8 °C, pulse 109 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, automated blood pressure 107/66 mm Hg confirmed manually, respiratory rate 41 breaths per minute with moderate intercostal retractions, and fingertip pulse oximetry fluctuating between 90 % and 91 % on ambient air. His skin was hot and flushed, mucous membranes appeared dry, and capillary refill was just over two seconds. Jugular venous pulsation rose 5 cm above the sternal angle at 45°, similar to prior heart-failure clinic examinations. Cardiac auscultation revealed a tachycardic S1 and S2 with a soft third sound but no new murmurs. Pulmonary examination disclosed dullness to percussion and coarse inspiratory crackles over the right middle and lower posterior lung zones; breath sounds were otherwise vesicular with no wheezes, and no asymmetry of diaphragmatic excursion was appreciated. The abdomen was soft and nontender with normal bowel sounds; no organomegaly was palpable. There was trace bilateral ankle edema unchanged from baseline. Screening neurologic assessment showed equal pupils, fluent speech, intact cranial nerves, and full strength in all extremities. Point-of-care capillary glucose measured 135 mg/dL. Peripheral venous blood was drawn immediately, and an arterial sample from the left radial artery was obtained within ten minutes of arrival while the patient remained on room air. Chemistry panel returned sodium 123 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 99 mEq/L, bicarbonate 25 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 43 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, the latter unchanged from baseline. Complete blood count revealed a hematocrit of 25 % with hemoglobin 8.3 g/dL and leukocytosis of 18.1 × 10⁹/L, 87 % segmented neutrophils. Arterial blood gas demonstrated pH 7.57, PaCO₂ 28 mm Hg, PaO₂ 84 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, consistent with an acute primary respiratory alkalosis. High-sensitivity troponin was below the assay threshold. A portable posterior-anterior and lateral chest radiograph obtained before any treatment showed a dense right lower-lobe consolidation with air bronchograms; the costophrenic angles remained sharp without blunting, and no fluid line or meniscus was visualized. Cardiac silhouette was mildly enlarged but unchanged from an outpatient film two months earlier, and pulmonary vascular markings were not engorged. Electrocardiography displayed sinus tachycardia at 108 beats per minute with nonspecific ST-T wave changes identical to prior tracings. Two sets of blood cultures, an expectorated sputum sample for Gram stain and culture, and a urine antigen assay for Streptococcus pneumoniae were collected before antimicrobial agents were ordered. At the moment this note is completed the patient is still breathing ambient air in a semi-erect position, has received no acetaminophen, no diuretics, no intravenous fluids, and no antibiotics, preserving the above findings as his untreated physiologic baseline.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Apply the Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI/PORT) using untreated admission findings.
- Demographics: male, age 48 = 48 points; no nursing-home residence = 0.
- Comorbidities: systolic heart failure = 10; no liver, cerebrovascular, or chronic renal disease = 0 each. Neoplastic disease adds 30 only if the prior seminoma is counted. Standard PSI counts active cancer or cancer diagnosed within the past year; his seminoma was treated 12 years ago without recurrence.
- Examination: respiratory rate 41/min (≥30) = 20. Normal mentation, systolic BP 107 (not <90), pulse 109 (not ≥125), and admission temperature 39.8 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40) = 0 each. The earlier workplace temperature is not the admission measurement.
- Labs and imaging: BUN 43 mg/dL (≥30) = 20; sodium 123 mEq/L (<130) = 20; hematocrit 25% (<30%) = 10. Arterial pH 7.57 (not <7.35), glucose 135 mg/dL (not ≥250), PaO₂ 84 mm Hg (not <60), and no pleural effusion = 0 each.
Standard PSI = 48 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 128. Counting the remote seminoma as neoplastic disease instead gives 128 + 30 = 158.
Final answer: 158
